title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
When choosing a book, price and reader ratings are often two useful pieces of information to consider. A highly rated book may seem appealing, but is it worth the price? On the other hand, the cheapest option may not necessarily provide the best reading experience.
This led me to a simple question:

Which book categories offer relatively highly rated books at lower prices?

To explore this question, I used web scraping to collect book information and compared prices and ratings across different categories.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
When choosing a book, price and reader ratings are often two useful pieces of information to consider. A highly rated book may seem appealing, but is it worth the price? On the other hand, the cheapest option may not necessarily provide the best reading experience.
This led me to a simple question:

Which book categories offer relatively highly rated books at lower prices?

To explore this question, I used web scraping to collect book information and compared prices and ratings across different categories.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
Collecting the Data
For this analysis, I scraped data from Books to Scrape, a website specifically designed for practicing web scraping.
Using the rvest package in R, I collected four pieces of information for each book:

title
category
price
star rating

Because the books are spread across multiple category pages, the scraping process also followed pagination links until all available books in each category were collected. I included short pauses between requests to avoid sending requests to the website too frequently.
After scraping the data, I converted prices from text into numeric values and transformed the star-rating labels into a numeric scale from 1 to 5.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
Comparing Book Categories
Since my research question focuses on categories rather than individual books, I summarized the data at the category level.
For each category, I calculated:

the number of books
average price
median price
average rating

One challenge was that category sizes varied substantially. Some categories contained only one or a few books, while the median category contained about 10 books. An average based on only one book could give a misleading impression of an entire category.
For the main comparison, I therefore focused on categories containing at least 10 books. This left 25 categories for analysis.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
What Counts as “Good Value”?
Rather than creating an arbitrary score such as rating divided by price, I used two simple benchmarks: the overall average book price and the overall average book rating.
I classified a category as meeting the good-value criteria when:

its average price was below the overall average book price, and
its average rating was above the overall average book rating.

This definition makes the tradeoff easy to interpret: I am looking for categories that are relatively less expensive while still receiving relatively stronger ratings.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
Price vs. Rating
The figure below compares average price and average rating across the 25 categories included in the analysis.

Each point represents one book category, and the size of the point reflects the number of books in that category. The vertical dashed line represents the overall average price, while the horizontal dashed line represents the overall average rating.
The area in the upper-left of the figure is especially interesting. Categories in this region have both lower-than-average prices and higher-than-average ratings, meaning they satisfy both of my good-value criteria.

The results reveal several different ways a category can provide value.
Humor has the highest average rating among the five categories, at 3.40 stars, while still maintaining a below-average price.
Historical Fiction also combines a relatively strong average rating of 3.23 with a below-average price. With 26 books in the category, its result is also based on a larger selection than Humor.
Mystery, meanwhile, has the lowest average price among the five categories at approximately £31.70. For readers who place greater emphasis on price, it therefore represents a particularly affordable option among the categories meeting both criteria.
Sequential Art and Science also fall within the good-value region, although their average ratings are closer to the overall rating benchmark.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
section: What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Do?
text:
What Should a Budget-Conscious Reader Do?
The analysis suggests that readers do not necessarily have to choose between lower prices and stronger ratings.
For readers who prioritize ratings, Humor may be worth exploring first because it has the highest average rating among the categories meeting the good-value criteria. Historical Fiction also offers a combination of relatively strong ratings and below-average prices across a larger number of books.
For readers who are particularly price-sensitive, Mystery may be worth exploring because it has the lowest average price among the five categories.
More broadly, the analysis shows why considering price and rating together can be more informative than simply searching for either the cheapest or the highest-rated category.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
Limitations
There are several limitations to keep in mind.
First, Books to Scrape is a website designed for web-scraping practice rather than a live bookstore. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as an illustration of how web-scraped data can support a purchasing decision rather than as current recommendations for the real book market.
Second, star ratings provide only a simple measure of book quality. They do not capture individual preferences, written reviews, popularity, or other factors that may influence whether a reader enjoys a book.
Finally, category sizes vary considerably. Although I limited the main analysis to categories with at least 10 books, averages can still be influenced by the composition and number of books within each category.

title: Finding the Best-Value Book Categories
text:
Conclusion
By combining web scraping with a simple price-and-rating comparison, I identified five book categories that have both below-average prices and above-average ratings: Humor, Historical Fiction, Sequential Art, Mystery, and Science.
The results also show that “value” depends on what a reader cares about most. Humor stands out for its relatively high average rating, while Mystery stands out for its relatively low average price.
More importantly, this project demonstrates how information collected from the web can be transformed into a practical decision-making tool. Instead of looking at price or ratings separately, combining the two provides a clearer way to narrow down the available choices.

text: Simpson’s Paradox is a statistical phenomenon in which a relationship observed within separate groups can change or even reverse when the groups are combined. title: How Can the Same Data Tell Two Different Stories? Understanding Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Introduction
When we look at data, we often expect the numbers to give us a clear answer. If Treatment A has a higher success rate than Treatment B for different groups of patients, it seems reasonable to conclude that Treatment A is better. However, this conclusion can change when we combine the groups together.
This surprising situation is called Simpson’s Paradox. Simpson’s Paradox occurs when a relationship appears in several separate groups but changes or even reverses when the groups are combined. The mathematics behind it is not necessarily difficult. What makes the paradox unintuitive is that the way we group the data can change the conclusion we draw from it.

title: How Can the Same Data Tell Two Different Stories? Understanding Simpson’s Paradox
text:
A Simple Example
Suppose a hospital is comparing two treatments, Treatment A and Treatment B. Patients can be divided into two groups: mild cases and severe cases.
For mild cases, suppose Treatment A has a success rate of \(90%\), while Treatment B has a success rate of \(80%\). Therefore, Treatment A performs better:
\[
90\% > 80\%.
\]
For severe cases, suppose Treatment A has a success rate of \(30%\), while Treatment B has a success rate of \(20%\). Again, Treatment A performs better:
\[
30\% > 20\%.
\]
At this point, it seems obvious that Treatment A is the better treatment.
However, suppose the number of patients receiving each treatment is very different. Treatment A is used mostly for severe cases, while Treatment B is used mostly for mild cases.
For Treatment A, suppose there are 100 mild cases and 900 severe cases. Its overall success rate is
\[
\frac{100(0.90)+900(0.30)}{1000}
=0.36
=36\%.
\]
For Treatment B, suppose there are 900 mild cases and 100 severe cases. Its overall success rate is
\[
\frac{900(0.80)+100(0.20)}{1000}
=0.74
=74\%.
\]
Now we get a surprising result. Treatment A performs better in both patient groups, but Treatment B has the higher overall success rate:
\[
36\% < 74\%.
\]
This is the key feature of Simpson’s Paradox.

title: How Can the Same Data Tell Two Different Stories? Understanding Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Why Does This Happen?
The key is that the two treatments have different proportions of mild and severe patients.
Mild patients are easier to treat, so having more mild patients naturally increases a treatment’s overall success rate. Treatment B has mostly mild patients, while Treatment A has mostly severe patients.
Therefore, the overall success rates are not simply comparing the quality of the two treatments. They are also reflecting the different compositions of the patient groups.
In other words, the overall success rate is a weighted average of the success rates in the different groups. The weights are determined by how many patients belong to each group.
For Treatment A, the calculation is
\[
0.10(90\%) + 0.90(30\%) = 36\%.
\]
For Treatment B, the calculation is
\[
0.90(80\%) + 0.10(20\%) = 74\%.
\]
These calculations show why the overall comparison can be different from the comparisons within each group.
This is the main intuition behind Simpson’s Paradox: an aggregate result can hide what is happening inside individual groups.

title: How Can the Same Data Tell Two Different Stories? Understanding Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Visualizing the Paradox
We can visualize the success rates of the two treatments. Figure Figure 1 shows the success rates for mild cases, severe cases, and the overall population.






Figure 1: Success Rates for Treatments A and B



The figure shows the paradox clearly. Within both the mild and severe groups, Treatment A has a higher success rate than Treatment B. However, when we look at the overall data, Treatment B has a much higher success rate.

title: How Can the Same Data Tell Two Different Stories? Understanding Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Why Should We Care?
Simpson’s Paradox is important because aggregate statistics are common in economics, business, medicine, and many other fields. Looking only at an overall average can sometimes lead to a misleading conclusion.
For example, when comparing two policies, companies, schools, or economic outcomes, we should consider whether important groups have different characteristics. A difference in the overall data may partly reflect differences in the composition of the groups rather than a true difference in performance.
This does not mean that aggregate statistics are always wrong. Instead, it means that we should understand what is behind an aggregate number before using it to make a conclusion.

title: How Can the Same Data Tell Two Different Stories? Understanding Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Conclusion
Simpson’s Paradox shows that the same data can tell different stories depending on how we group it. A result that appears true in the aggregate may disappear or even reverse when we examine smaller groups.
The important lesson is simple: before drawing conclusions from aggregate data, we should look inside the groups that make up that data.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
text:
The gender wage gap is often summarized by a single number, but differences in earnings may vary across different groups of workers. Education is one important dimension to consider when examining these differences.
This led me to a simple question:

How does the gender wage gap vary across education levels in the United States?

To explore this question, I used individual-level data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) through IPUMS. I focus on employed adults ages 25–64 from 2015 to 2025 and compare women’s and men’s weekly earnings across different education levels.
Rather than looking only at the overall gender wage gap, I examine how the female-to-male weekly earnings ratio changes over time and how it differs across education groups.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
text:
The gender wage gap is often summarized by a single number, but differences in earnings may vary across different groups of workers. Education is one important dimension to consider when examining these differences.
This led me to a simple question:

How does the gender wage gap vary across education levels in the United States?

To explore this question, I used individual-level data from the Current Population Survey (CPS) through IPUMS. I focus on employed adults ages 25–64 from 2015 to 2025 and compare women’s and men’s weekly earnings across different education levels.
Rather than looking only at the overall gender wage gap, I examine how the female-to-male weekly earnings ratio changes over time and how it differs across education groups.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
text:
Collecting and Preparing the Data
For this analysis, I used the Current Population Survey (CPS) provided through IPUMS.
The sample includes employed adults between ages 25 and 64 from 2015 through 2025. I use EARNWEEK2 to measure weekly earnings and EARNWT as the earnings weight.
I restricted the sample to individuals with valid and positive weekly earnings and positive earnings weights. I also divided education into five groups:

Less than high school
High school
Some college / Associate
Bachelor’s
Advanced degree

Because CPS data are survey data, I used the earnings weights when calculating average weekly earnings. This allows the results to better represent the population rather than treating every survey observation as equally representative.
For each year and education group, I calculated the weighted average weekly earnings for men and women.
I then calculated the female-to-male weekly earnings ratio:
\[
\text{Female-to-Male Earnings Ratio}
=
\frac{\text{Female Mean Weekly Earnings}}
{\text{Male Mean Weekly Earnings}}
\]
For example, a ratio of 0.75 means that women’s average weekly earnings are 75% of men’s average weekly earnings.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
section: The Overall Gender Wage Gap Over Time
text:
The Overall Gender Wage Gap Over Time
I first looked at the overall female-to-male weekly earnings ratio from 2015 to 2025.

The overall ratio was 76.1% in 2015. It gradually increased during the following years and reached 80.6% in 2022. After 2022, however, the ratio declined, reaching 73.9% in 2025.
This means that the overall gender earnings gap did not move steadily in one direction during the period. Instead, the ratio improved during the earlier part of the sample before declining in the later years.
This pattern is useful as a starting point, but the overall ratio may hide differences between workers with different levels of education. I therefore next examine the gender earnings gap across education groups.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
section: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Differ Across Education Levels?
text:
How Does the Gender Wage Gap Differ Across Education Levels?
To examine differences across education groups, I calculated the weighted average weekly earnings for men and women within each education category and then calculated the female-to-male earnings ratio.

The results show differences across all five education groups.
The female-to-male weekly earnings ratios are approximately:

67.9% for workers with less than a high school education
69.9% for workers with a high school education
71.3% for workers with some college or an associate degree
73.8% for workers with a bachelor’s degree
76.0% for workers with an advanced degree

In this sample, the female-to-male earnings ratio is higher among workers with higher levels of education.
For example, women with an advanced degree earn about 76% as much as men with an advanced degree on average, compared with about 68% among workers with less than a high school education.
This suggests that education is an important dimension to consider when examining the gender earnings gap. Looking only at an overall average would hide these differences across education groups.
However, this analysis is descriptive. The results do not show that obtaining more education causes the gender earnings gap to become smaller. Education may also be associated with other factors such as occupation, industry, work experience, and hours worked.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
section: How Do Education-Specific Gaps Change Over Time?
text:
How Do Education-Specific Gaps Change Over Time?
The previous comparison combines data from 2015 through 2025. To examine whether the differences across education groups are stable over time, I calculated the female-to-male earnings ratio separately for each education group and each year.

Figure 3 shows how the female-to-male earnings ratio changes over time for each education group.
The lines allow us to compare both differences between education groups and changes within each group over time. The education-specific ratios fluctuate from year to year, and the lines sometimes cross each other. This means that the relationship between education level and the gender earnings gap is not constant over the entire sample period.
One particularly noticeable pattern is the decline in the advanced-degree ratio after 2022. The ratio reaches about 81% in 2022 but falls to about 67% by 2025.
This highlights why it is useful to examine the data from multiple perspectives. Figure 1 shows the overall trend, Figure 2 shows differences across education levels, and Figure 3 combines both dimensions.
Together, the three figures provide a more detailed picture of the gender earnings gap than a single overall statistic would provide.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
section: What Can We Learn from the Data?
text:
What Can We Learn from the Data?
The analysis reveals three main patterns.
First, the overall female-to-male weekly earnings ratio changed substantially over the 2015–2025 period. It increased from 76.1% in 2015 to 80.6% in 2022 before falling to 73.9% in 2025.
Second, the gender earnings gap varies across education levels. Over the full sample period, the female-to-male earnings ratio ranges from approximately 67.9% among workers with less than a high school education to 76.0% among workers with an advanced degree.
Third, education-specific earnings ratios also vary over time. Therefore, the gender earnings gap is not a single fixed number that applies equally to all workers.
These results show the value of breaking down labor-market data by characteristics such as education. An overall average can provide a useful summary, but it may conceal meaningful differences between groups.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
text:
Limitations
There are several limitations to this analysis.
First, the analysis is descriptive rather than causal. The results show an association between education level and the female-to-male earnings ratio, but they do not establish that education itself causes differences in the gender earnings gap.
Second, the outcome variable is weekly earnings rather than hourly wages. Weekly earnings can be affected by the number of hours worked, so differences in hours may contribute to the observed gender earnings gap.
Third, workers within the same education group can still differ in many other characteristics, including occupation, industry, age, and work experience. These factors are not controlled for in this descriptive analysis.
Finally, the earnings data are nominal. The female-to-male ratio within each year is not directly affected by common inflation, but changes in nominal earnings levels over time should not be interpreted as changes in real purchasing power.

title: How Does the Gender Wage Gap Vary Across Education Levels?
text:
Conclusion
Using CPS microdata from 2015 to 2025, I examined how the gender gap in weekly earnings varies across education levels and over time.
The overall female-to-male weekly earnings ratio increased from 76.1% in 2015 to 80.6% in 2022, before declining to 73.9% in 2025. Across education groups, the ratio ranged from 67.9% among workers with less than a high school education to 76.0% among workers with an advanced degree.
The results suggest that the gender earnings gap is not uniform across the labor market. Education level provides one useful way to uncover differences that are not visible in the overall average.
More broadly, this project demonstrates how individual-level survey data can be transformed into clear visualizations that help answer an economic question. By combining trends over time with differences across education groups, we can obtain a more detailed understanding of the gender earnings gap in the United States.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
text:
Buying a home is one of the largest financial decisions many households make. But whether a home is affordable depends on more than its price. Household income determines how much a family can reasonably spend, while mortgage rates determine the cost of borrowing. A home can therefore become harder to afford even if its price is no longer rising, especially when interest rates increase.
This raises the question:
How has housing affordability in the United States changed as home prices, mortgage rates, and household incomes have evolved since 2000?
To explore this question, I use U.S. housing, mortgage, and income data from Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) covering 2000 through 2025. I focus on three parts of the affordability story. First, I compare the growth of home prices with household income. Second, I examine changes in mortgage rates. Finally, I combine home prices, borrowing costs, and income into a simplified measure of mortgage burden.
Together, these three perspectives show that housing affordability cannot be understood from home prices alone.

text:

A home can therefore become harder to afford even if its price is no longer rising, especially when interest rates increase.
This raises the question:
How has housing affordability in the United States changed as home prices, mortgage rates, and household incomes have evolved since 2000?
To explore this question, I use U.S. housing, mortgage, and income data from Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) covering 2000 through 2025. I focus on three parts of the affordability story. First, I compare the growth of home prices with household income. Second, I examine changes in mortgage rates. Finally, I combine home prices, borrowing costs, and income into a simplified measure of mortgage burden.
Together, these three perspectives show that housing affordability cannot be understood from home prices alone.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
text:
Data and Method
I collected four series programmatically from FRED using the fredr package in R:

the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (CSUSHPINSA);
the 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States (MORTGAGE30US);
Median Household Income in the United States (MEHOINUSA646N); and
the Median Sales Price of New Houses Sold for the United States (MSPUS).

These series are reported at different frequencies. The home price index is monthly, mortgage rates are weekly, median new-home sale prices are quarterly, and household income is annual. To make the series comparable, I converted them to annual observations. I calculated annual averages for the home price index, mortgage rate, and median new-home sale price, while household income was already available annually.
For the first comparison, I reindexed both home prices and household income so that their annual values in 2000 equal 100. This allows the two series to be compared in terms of relative growth even though they are originally measured in different units.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
section: Home Prices Have Outpaced Household Income
text:
Home Prices Have Outpaced Household Income
The first part of the affordability story is the relationship between home prices and household income.

Both series begin at 100 in 2000, but they follow increasingly different paths over the next 25 years.
Home prices increased rapidly during the early 2000s, reaching an indexed value of roughly 176 in 2006 before declining during and after the housing market downturn. Household income grew much more gradually over the same period.
The gap became especially pronounced after 2020. By 2025, the home price index had reached approximately 314, compared with about 208 for median household income.
In other words, relative to their 2000 levels, home prices more than tripled while nominal median household income roughly doubled. The comparison suggests that the price of housing has increased substantially faster than the income available to purchase it.
However, this price-income gap does not provide a complete measure of affordability. Most buyers finance at least part of a home purchase with a mortgage. As a result, the interest rate attached to that mortgage can substantially change the monthly cost of purchasing the same home.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
section: Falling Mortgage Rates Initially Helped Buyers
text:
Falling Mortgage Rates Initially Helped Buyers
The second figure adds the cost of borrowing to the story.

Mortgage rates generally declined over the first two decades of the period. The annual average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was approximately 8.05% in 2000. By 2010, it had fallen to about 4.69%, and it reached approximately 2.96% in 2021.
This decline matters for affordability because a lower interest rate reduces the monthly principal-and-interest payment associated with a given mortgage balance. In other words, falling rates helped offset some of the affordability pressure created by rising home prices.
The situation changed dramatically after 2021.
The annual average mortgage rate increased from 2.96% in 2021 to 5.34% in 2022, and then to 6.81% in 2023. Rates remained relatively high afterward, averaging about 6.72% in 2024 and 6.60% in 2025.
This sharp increase shows why looking only at home prices can be misleading. Even if the price of a home stays constant, financing that home becomes substantially more expensive when mortgage rates rise.
The next step is therefore to combine these factors rather than examine them separately.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
section: Combining Home Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Income
text:
Combining Home Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Income
To capture the interaction between prices, interest rates, and income, I constructed a simplified measure of estimated mortgage burden.
For each year, I assume that a household purchases a median-priced new home with a 20% down payment and finances the remaining 80% with a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. I use the annual average mortgage rate to calculate the monthly principal-and-interest payment.
I then calculate:
\[
\text{Estimated Mortgage Burden}
=
\frac{\text{Annual Principal-and-Interest Payment}}
{\text{Median Household Income}}
\times 100
\]
A higher value means that the estimated mortgage payment would consume a larger share of median household income and therefore indicates lower affordability under these standardized assumptions.

This figure reveals a pattern that is not obvious from home prices alone.
In 2000, estimated mortgage burden was approximately 28.3% of median household income. It increased to about 30.4% in 2006, around the peak of the pre-financial-crisis housing boom.
Afterward, the estimated burden generally declined. By 2012, it had fallen to approximately 21.1%, and in 2020 it reached its lowest value in the sample at about 19.8%.
This is particularly interesting because homes in 2020 were much more expensive than they had been in 2000. The first figure shows that the home price index had already risen to roughly twice its 2000 level. Yet estimated mortgage burden was lower than in 2000.
The mortgage-rate figure helps explain why. By 2020, the annual average 30-year mortgage rate had fallen to only about 3.11%. Low borrowing costs partially offset the effect of higher home prices.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
text:
The Affordability Shock After 2021
The clearest change occurs between 2021 and 2023.
Estimated mortgage burden increased from 21.8% in 2021 to 31.1% in 2022 and then reached 33.1% in 2023, the highest value in the 2000–2025 period.
That is an increase of approximately 11.3 percentage points in just two years.
The timing is important. Home prices had already risen sharply by 2021, but mortgage rates were still historically low. Once mortgage rates increased in 2022 and 2023, buyers faced both elevated home prices and much higher financing costs at the same time.
For example, the annual average median new-home sale price was approximately $383,000 in 2021, with an average mortgage rate of 2.96%. Under the standardized assumptions used here, the estimated monthly principal-and-interest payment was about $1,285.
In 2023, the annual average median new-home sale price was approximately $426,525 and the average mortgage rate had increased to 6.81%. The estimated monthly payment rose to approximately $2,226.
This means that the standardized monthly mortgage payment increased by roughly $941, or about 73%, between 2021 and 2023.
Household income increased over the same period, but not enough to offset the combined effect of higher home prices and substantially higher interest rates. As a result, the estimated mortgage burden rose sharply.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
section: Lower Home Prices Do Not Necessarily Mean Affordable Homes
text:
Lower Home Prices Do Not Necessarily Mean Affordable Homes
The final years of the data provide another useful example.
The annual average of quarterly median new-home sale prices declined from approximately $432,950 in 2022 to $415,400 in 2025. At the same time, median household income continued to increase.
These changes helped reduce estimated mortgage burden from its 2023 peak of 33.1% to 29.1% in 2025.
However, the burden remained considerably higher than the 19.8% recorded in 2020 and the 21.8% recorded in 2021.
The reason is that mortgage rates remained elevated. The average rate in 2025 was approximately 6.60%, more than twice the 2021 average of 2.96%.
This illustrates an important economic point: a decline in home prices does not automatically restore housing affordability. When borrowing costs remain high, buyers may still face large monthly payments even if home prices have fallen from their peak.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
section: What Do the Three Figures Tell Us?
text:
What Do the Three Figures Tell Us?
Taken together, the three visualizations tell a consistent story.
First, home prices have grown substantially faster than median household income since 2000. By 2025, the home price index stood at roughly 314 relative to its 2000 level, compared with about 208 for household income.
Second, falling mortgage rates helped offset some of this growing price-income gap for much of the 2000s and 2010s. This helps explain why the estimated mortgage burden could decline even while home prices were increasing.
Third, the sharp rise in mortgage rates after 2021 removed much of that offset. Potential buyers were suddenly facing the combination of elevated home prices and much more expensive borrowing. The result was a rapid increase in estimated mortgage burden, which peaked at 33.1% in 2023.
The analysis therefore suggests that housing affordability is best understood as the interaction of three factors:
home prices + borrowing costs + household income.
Looking at any one of these variables in isolation can miss an important part of the story.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
text:
Limitations
The estimated mortgage burden used in this analysis is a standardized measure rather than an official housing affordability index.
Several assumptions are necessary to make the comparison consistent over time. The calculation assumes a 20% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. It also assumes that the buyer purchases a median-priced new home and receives the annual average mortgage rate.
The calculation includes only mortgage principal and interest. It does not include property taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA fees, maintenance costs, closing costs, or other expenses associated with homeownership. Actual mortgage rates and down payments also vary across borrowers depending on factors such as credit history and financial circumstances.
In addition, the dollar home-price series used in the mortgage calculation represents the median sales price of new houses sold, rather than all existing and new homes in the United States.
Finally, the household income series is measured in current dollars. The indexed comparison in the first figure therefore shows the relative growth of nominal household income and the home price index; it should not be interpreted as a measure of real income growth.
Despite these limitations, applying the same assumptions in every year provides a useful standardized comparison of how the financial conditions facing a hypothetical homebuyer have changed over time.

title: Priced Out? How U.S. Housing Affordability Has Changed Since 2000
text:
Conclusion
Housing affordability in the United States has changed substantially since 2000, but the story is more complicated than simply saying that home prices increased.
Home prices grew much faster than median household income, creating increasing pressure on affordability. For many years, however, declining mortgage rates partially offset that pressure by making it cheaper to finance a home. That changed after 2021, when mortgage rates rose rapidly while home prices remained elevated.
Under the standardized assumptions used in this analysis, estimated mortgage burden increased from 21.8% of median household income in 2021 to 33.1% in 2023. Although the burden declined to 29.1% by 2025, it remained substantially above the levels observed during the low-rate years.
The main takeaway is that housing affordability cannot be evaluated from home prices alone. What ultimately matters for a financed home purchase is not only the price of the house, but also the interest rate used to finance it and the income available to make the payments.

Geographic Patterns in Household Income






Figure 1: Median household income by census tract in Philadelphia. Gray tracts have no valid income estimate.



Figure 1 (Figure 1) shows that income is not evenly distributed across Philadelphia. Several relatively high-income tracts appear near one another in the northwestern part of the city, visible in green and yellow. By contrast, many tracts in the central and southwestern portions of the map appear in darker purple, indicating lower median household incomes. Other parts of the city contain a mix of income levels, underscoring variation even across nearby tracts.
The gap between the highest and lowest observed tract median incomes is approximately $209,781, and the highest estimate is about 12.7 times the lowest. These comparisons indicate substantial differences in the typical household income of different census tracts. They do not mean that the highest-income household in Philadelphia earns 12.7 times the lowest-income household: the unit being compared is the tract median, not individual household income.
The visual concentration of similarly colored neighboring tracts suggests a possible spatial clustering of income levels. This matters because a citywide summary could conceal geographically concentrated differences in economic resources. However, a map alone cannot establish whether the clustering is statistically significant or identify what caused it. Factors such as housing costs, employment opportunities, and historical development may be relevant hypotheses, but testing them would require additional data and analysis.

section: How Unequal Are Tract-Level Income Estimates?

How Unequal Are Tract-Level Income Estimates?






Figure 2: Distribution of median household income across Philadelphia census tracts. The red dashed line marks the median across tracts ($62,083).



Figure 2 (Figure 2) complements the map by showing the overall distribution of tract median incomes. Many tracts fall roughly between $30,000 and $100,000, while a smaller number have much higher values. The long upper tail gives the distribution a right-skewed shape.
The mean tract median income ($68,707) exceeds the median across tracts ($62,083), consistent with a relatively small number of high-income tracts pulling the mean upward. The standard deviation of approximately $32,658 also indicates considerable dispersion across geographic areas.
The histogram tells us how income estimates are distributed across tracts, but it does not show where those tracts are located. Conversely, the map highlights geographic patterns but makes the overall shape of the distribution harder to see. Using both figures provides a more complete description of spatial income differences.

title: Mapping Income Inequality in Philadelphia
text:
Conclusion
Philadelphia’s census tracts exhibit substantial variation in median household income. The GIS map suggests that relatively high- and low-income tracts are not randomly scattered to the eye: some appear in geographically concentrated groups, especially a higher-income cluster in the northwest and lower-income areas across parts of the center and southwest. The histogram adds evidence that the distribution of tract medians is right-skewed, with a relatively small upper-income tail.
The central lesson is that geography matters when describing economic inequality. A single citywide income measure cannot show the extent or location of differences between census tracts. Mapping those differences offers a useful starting point for asking more targeted questions about housing, opportunity, and access to services.

Limitations and Next Steps
This is a descriptive, not causal, analysis. ACS figures are survey estimates with sampling uncertainty; 33 tracts lack valid estimates in this dataset. Census tracts differ in population and household counts, so unweighted tract summaries should not be interpreted as citywide household income statistics. Median income within each tract also does not measure inequality within that tract. Finally, the apparent clustering has not been tested with a formal spatial statistic such as Moran’s I.
A future extension could compare income with housing costs, transit access, or other neighborhood characteristics and test spatial autocorrelation explicitly.

title: Mapping Income Disparities Across Philadelphia
text:
A single income statistic cannot tell us how economic resources are distributed across a city. Two cities could have the same citywide median household income but very different differences between neighborhoods. Even the same set of neighborhood income values could be arranged differently: lower-income areas might be dispersed or located next to one another. Understanding both the size and the geography of these differences is therefore important for describing urban economic conditions.
This post asks: How much does median household income vary across Philadelphia census tracts, and what does its spatial arrangement add to our understanding of those differences? I use a choropleth map to examine location and a histogram to examine the distribution of tract median incomes. The analysis concerns income disparities between census tracts, rather than inequality among all individual households or inequality within each tract.

title: Mapping Income Disparities Across Philadelphia
section: Where Are Higher- and Lower-Income Tracts Located?
text:
Where Are Higher- and Lower-Income Tracts Located?






Figure 1: Median household income by Philadelphia census tract, using 2020–2024 ACS estimates expressed in 2024 dollars. Purple indicates lower values, green and yellow higher values, and gray no valid income value in the analysis dataset.



Figure 1 shows substantial geographic variation. Several neighboring tracts in the northwest have relatively high median incomes, including the map’s brightest yellow tract. However, higher incomes are not confined to the northwest: another visible concentration of green and teal tracts appears toward the eastern side of the city’s southern portion. Many tracts across the interior and southwest have lower values, shown in dark purple. The northeast includes a mix of intermediate income levels. These are broad visual descriptions, rather than formally defined regional comparisons.
The important spatial finding is that similar income levels sometimes extend across neighboring tract boundaries. Lower-income areas are therefore not represented only by isolated tracts, and higher-income areas are not distributed uniformly throughout the city. This suggests that the geographic scale of income disparities can extend beyond a single tract. A tract-by-tract ranking would identify high and low values, but would miss whether those values form adjoining areas.
There are also visible transitions between nearby tracts with different colors. This cautions against treating a broad part of Philadelphia as economically uniform. A regional label can conceal local differences, just as a citywide statistic can conceal differences between regions. The map supports examining multiple geographic scales rather than assigning one income description to the entire city or to a large section of it.
These patterns are consistent with possible spatial clustering, but the map alone does not establish statistically significant spatial autocorrelation. Nor does it establish why the differences exist. Residential sorting, housing costs, employment patterns, and historical development are possible explanations to investigate, not findings demonstrated by this income map.

title: Mapping Income Disparities Across Philadelphia
section: How Widely Do Tract Median Incomes Vary?
text:
How Widely Do Tract Median Incomes Vary?






Figure 2: Distribution of median household income across the 375 Philadelphia census tracts with valid estimates. Values are in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars and represent 2020–2024 ACS period estimates. The red dashed line marks the median across tracts, $62,083.



Figure 2 shows a right-skewed distribution: many tract medians fall approximately between $30,000 and $100,000, while relatively few extend far above that range. This is not a picture of two equally large groups separated neatly into rich and poor areas. Instead, tract incomes span a broad range, with a smaller upper-income tail. The histogram therefore adds an important qualification to the map: visually striking high-income tracts should not be mistaken for the income level of a typical tract.
The mean of tract medians, $68,707, is $6,624, or approximately 10.7%, above the median across tracts, $62,083. Together with the visible upper tail, this indicates that higher-income tracts pull the mean upward. Using only the mean would therefore give a higher numerical benchmark than the middle tract’s income estimate. The choice of summary statistic changes how a reader understands a “typical” tract, although neither statistic describes the typical Philadelphia household.
The standard deviation of $32,658 is approximately 47.5% of the mean of tract medians, indicating substantial dispersion relative to the scale of the values. At the extremes, the highest tract median is approximately 12.7 times the lowest, a difference of $209,781. This ratio compares two tract-level estimates—not the richest and poorest households—and depends on only two observations. It illustrates the observed range but does not establish how widespread differences of that magnitude are. Sampling uncertainty also makes precise rankings of extreme tracts less secure than their displayed estimates might suggest.

title: Mapping Income Disparities Across Philadelphia
section: What the Two Figures Reveal Together
text:
What the Two Figures Reveal Together
The figures answer complementary parts of the research question. The histogram establishes that tract incomes vary widely and that the upper end contains relatively few tracts. The map shows where those incomes occur and suggests that some similar values occupy adjoining areas. The distribution describes the magnitude and frequency of income differences; the map reveals their geographic arrangement.
One way to understand the map’s contribution is to imagine reassigning the observed income values among Philadelphia’s tracts. The histogram, mean, median, and range would remain unchanged, but the locations of lower- and higher-income areas could change completely. The observed map therefore contains information that the distribution cannot supply: where income differences are concentrated and where nearby areas have different median incomes. This is why a spatial analysis adds more than a geographic illustration of a summary table.
The figures also use different visual weights. A large tract occupies more map space than a small tract, while each contributes one observation to the histogram. Neither figure weights tracts by the number of households. Consequently, a large colored region is not necessarily home to a large share of Philadelphia’s households, and the proportion of low-income tracts is not the proportion of low-income households. Land area, tract counts, and household counts answer different questions. This distinction is essential before using the map to assess the scale of potential service needs.
For practical use, the map can identify adjoining lower-income areas that warrant closer investigation, rather than relying on one citywide benchmark. However, lower median income alone does not demonstrate inadequate transit, poor public services, or high housing-cost burdens. Those are separate outcomes. The present results help identify where to investigate, while additional household, cost, and service data are needed to determine what intervention, if any, is appropriate.

title: Mapping Income Disparities Across Philadelphia
text:
Limitations and Next Steps
First, ACS incomes are survey estimates. Without examining their margins of error, small differences between tracts should not be treated as precise differences, and the highest and lowest estimates should not be interpreted as definitive rankings. Second, 33 tracts lack valid values in the cleaned dataset. Their absence limits coverage; without checking the source values and join results, it is not possible to determine whether they reflect unavailable estimates, cleaning decisions, or unmatched records, or how their exclusion affects the pattern.
Third, these results concern differences between tract medians. Two tracts can have the same median while having very different internal income distributions. The analysis therefore cannot measure total household income inequality or establish how much of it occurs within versus between tracts. Fourth, the spatial descriptions depend on the chosen tract boundaries, and apparent clustering has not been tested with a statistic such as Moran’s I. Finally, the data provide one pooled period, so they do not establish whether disparities are increasing, declining, or reflecting recent neighborhood change.
A useful extension would first examine ACS margins of error and audit the missing values, then add household counts to distinguish the geographic extent of lower-income areas from the number of households living in them. Housing-cost measures could assess whether income differences correspond to different financial pressures. A spatial autocorrelation test could separately evaluate whether the apparent clustering provides evidence against a specified spatial randomness benchmark. Each extension addresses a specific uncertainty in the present interpretation.

title: Mapping Income Disparities Across Philadelphia
text:
Conclusion
Philadelphia’s tract-level income differences are substantial, but their significance lies in more than the distance between the highest and lowest estimates. The histogram shows a broad distribution with a relatively small upper-income tail; the mean of tract medians consequently exceeds the middle tract’s estimate. The map adds that some similar income levels appear in adjoining areas, with visible higher-income concentrations in parts of the northwest and the eastern side of the southern portion of the city, alongside lower-income areas across much of the interior and southwest.
The central takeaway is that understanding Philadelphia’s income disparities requires both a distribution and a location. A summary statistic cannot show the spatial extent of lower-income areas, and a map alone cannot show how common particular income levels are. Together, the figures reveal differences that are both economically substantial and geographically patterned, while preserving an important distinction between tract-level observations and household-level welfare.
The appropriate implication is to use these patterns to guide more targeted investigation. Identifying adjoining lower-income tracts can help define where to examine financial pressures and service needs, but allocating resources requires evidence about household numbers, estimation uncertainty, costs, and existing services. The analysis thus provides a geographic starting point for understanding disparities, rather than a causal explanation or a complete policy prescription.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Do children from higher-earning families tend to earn more as adults? Answering this question requires two tasks: identifying parents and children in longitudinal records, and measuring earnings in a way that reflects long-run economic status. A single year can be unusually good or bad, and earnings change as people enter the labor market or retire.
Research question: How can SQL inside Python match mothers and adult children in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), and how sensitive is the estimated intergenerational earnings elasticity (IGE) to using one year versus several years of earnings?
This tutorial moves from identifiers to SQL joins, constructs individual earnings, uses SQL aggregation to average earnings, estimates the IGE, and examines measurement-year and maternal-age sensitivity.
The analysis concerns birth mothers’ and adult children’s individual labor earnings, not total parental household income or causal effects.

title: How Much Does a Mother’s Income Predict Her Child’s Earnings?
text:
One of the central questions in economics is whether children can achieve economic outcomes independently of their parents’ circumstances. If children from higher-income families consistently earn more as adults, economic advantages may persist across generations. If the relationship is weaker, parental earnings may be less predictive of children’s economic outcomes.
This blog post investigates the following research question:
How strongly are parents’ earnings associated with their adult children’s earnings, and how does this relationship change when we measure income over multiple years?
I use data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), a longitudinal household survey that follows individuals and families over time. By connecting family relationships with individual earnings records, I examine the association between maternal labor earnings and adult children’s labor earnings.
Although the broader economic question concerns parental income, the empirical analysis focuses specifically on mother-child pairs, because the parent-child linkage constructed for this project identifies mothers.
The analysis has three objectives:

Estimate the association between mothers’ and adult children’s earnings using a single income year.
Examine whether averaging earnings across multiple survey waves changes the estimated relationship.
Investigate how restricting mothers to working ages affects the results.

The findings highlight an important methodological lesson: estimates of intergenerational income persistence depend not only on the underlying economic relationship but also on how income is measured and which individuals are included in the sample.

title: How Much Does a Mother’s Income Predict Her Child’s Earnings?
text:
Data: Following Families Across Generations

Data Source
The analysis uses the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), which provides longitudinal information on individuals, family relationships, and economic outcomes.
Three components are combined:

Individual data: Person identifiers, family membership, age, and relationship to the household reference person.
Parent Identification File (PID): Identifiers linking children to their mothers.
Family income data: Labor earnings for household reference persons and spouses.

I examine four PSID survey waves: 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023. These correspond to income reference years 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022.


Data Preparation and SQL Matching
The raw files have different structures and identifiers, making direct comparison difficult.
I first cleaned and reshaped the individual records from wide to long format. Each observation in the resulting dataset represents one person in one survey year.
Next, I used SQL joins to connect individuals across datasets.
An INNER JOIN matched mother-child identifiers from the Parent Identification File with individuals in the PSID data. This produced 41,839 preliminary mother-child pairs.
A separate LEFT JOIN connected individual-year records with family income using family identifiers and survey years. This produced 96,340 matched person-year records.
Because family income variables identify earnings for particular household roles, I assigned reference-person labor earnings only to reference persons and spouse labor earnings only to legal spouses. I did not automatically assign household earnings to other family members.
This distinction matters because household income is not the same as an individual’s labor earnings.


Constructing the Analysis Sample
I restricted the analysis to mother-child pairs where:

The child was at least 25 years old in 2023.
The mother’s age was observed.
Both individuals had positive labor earnings for the relevant regression.

The resulting single-year sample contains 1,178 mother-child pairs.
For the multi-year analysis, I calculated each person’s average positive labor earnings across the available survey waves and required at least two positive-income observations for both the mother and child.
This produced 1,602 mother-child pairs.
These restrictions improve the consistency of the earnings comparison, but they also introduce selection concerns. In particular, the analysis excludes individuals without positive observed earnings in the relevant periods.

title: How Much Does a Mother’s Income Predict Her Child’s Earnings?
text:
Methodology: Measuring Intergenerational Earnings Persistence

The Intergenerational Earnings Elasticity
A common measure of intergenerational economic persistence is the Intergenerational Earnings Elasticity (IGE).
The standard model is:
\[
\ln(Y_{\text{child},i})
=
\alpha
+
\beta \ln(Y_{\text{parent},i})
+
\varepsilon_i
\]
where:

\(Y_{\text{child},i}\) is the adult child’s earnings.
\(Y_{\text{parent},i}\) is the parent’s earnings.
\(\alpha\) is the regression intercept.
\(\beta\) is the intergenerational earnings elasticity.
\(\varepsilon_i\) captures other factors associated with the child’s earnings.

Because this project matches mothers to children, the estimated specification is:
\[
\ln(Y_{\text{child},i})
=
\alpha
+
\beta \ln(Y_{\text{mother},i})
+
\varepsilon_i
\]
The coefficient \(\beta\) measures the percentage association between maternal and child earnings.
For example, if \(\beta = 0.15\), a 10% difference in maternal earnings is associated with approximately a 1.5% difference in adult child earnings.
A higher positive IGE generally indicates stronger earnings persistence across generations and, under appropriate measurement and sampling assumptions, lower intergenerational earnings mobility.
However, IGE is an association rather than a causal estimate. It does not establish that increasing a mother’s earnings would directly cause her child to earn more.


Why Compare Single-Year and Multi-Year Earnings?
Annual labor earnings fluctuate because of job transitions, temporary unemployment, changes in working hours, and other short-term events.
Consequently, earnings observed in a single year may be an imperfect measure of an individual’s longer-term earning capacity.
To examine this issue, I estimate two versions of the IGE:
Single-Year IGE
Uses labor earnings reported in the 2023 survey, corresponding to the 2022 income year.
Multi-Year IGE
Uses average positive labor earnings from the 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023 survey waves, requiring at least two positive-income observations for each generation.
Multi-year averaging may reduce the influence of temporary earnings fluctuations. However, the available observations cover only four waves, and the averages are not inflation-adjusted.
Moreover, averaging only positive-income years does not capture periods of zero earnings.


Comparing a Common Sample
The single-year and multi-year specifications have different sample sizes. Therefore, changes in the estimated IGE could reflect either differences in income measurement or differences in sample composition.
To make the comparison more informative, I also estimate both specifications using the same 1,027 mother-child pairs.
This common-sample comparison holds the set of individuals constant, although it does not eliminate every source of measurement bias.
The regressions are estimated using ordinary least squares (OLS), with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

The single-year regression produces an estimated IGE of:
\[

The 95% confidence interval is approximately [-0.0030, 0.0836], and the regression has an \(R^2\) of 0.0026.
The estimated relationship is positive but small. The confidence interval includes zero, meaning that the single-year estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero at the conventional 5% significance level.
The low \(R^2\) indicates that maternal earnings alone explain very little of the observed variation in adult children’s log earnings in this sample.
One possible explanation is that a single income year contains substantial short-term variation unrelated to long-run economic position. However, measurement noise is not the only possible explanation for the weak association.

Nevertheless, the estimated relationship remains economically modest, and the model explains only a small fraction of variation in children’s earnings.
Importantly, the multi-year sample contains more observations than the single-year sample. Thus, the difference between these two estimates cannot be attributed solely to averaging.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: 8. Discussion: What Do These Results Tell Us?
text:
8. Discussion: What Do These Results Tell Us?
Three findings are particularly important.

First, Accurate Family Matching Is Essential
Intergenerational analysis begins with identifying the correct relatives.
Using stable individual identifiers and SQL joins prevents researchers from incorrectly matching individuals based only on current household membership.
SQL is therefore not simply a technical convenience. It determines which parent–child relationships enter the analysis.


Second, Income Measurement Affects Estimated Mobility
Within the common sample of 1,027 mother–child pairs, the single-year IGE is 0.0322, compared with 0.0641 using multi-year earnings.
Although this difference is not statistically significant in the paired bootstrap, it demonstrates the importance of checking whether results depend on the chosen income measure.
The balanced-sample analysis reinforces this concern: single-year estimates vary across earnings years even when sample composition is held constant.


Third, Averaging Is Useful but Not a Complete Solution
Multi-year averaging can reduce the influence of temporary income shocks.
However, it does not automatically remove life-cycle bias.
If observed earnings are concentrated near retirement, averaging several low-earnings years may still underestimate long-run earning capacity.
A longer income history measured during representative working ages would provide a better approximation of permanent economic status.


Limitations
Several limitations should be considered.

Maternal earnings only: The analysis excludes paternal earnings and total parental household resources.
Positive-income selection: Zero-income observations are excluded from log-income regressions and positive-income averages.
Limited observation window: Four intermittent earnings years do not represent entire careers.
Nominal earnings: Multi-year averages are not inflation-adjusted.
Survey representativeness: PSID survey weights are not incorporated.
Statistical dependence: HC1 standard errors do not account for clustering among siblings or mothers.
Noncausal interpretation: The estimated IGE measures association, not the causal effect of maternal earnings on children’s outcomes.

These limitations also help explain why the estimates should not be interpreted as nationally representative measures of intergenerational mobility.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
9. Conclusion
This tutorial demonstrates how SQL within Python can be used to construct a longitudinal mother–child earnings dataset and estimate intergenerational earnings elasticity.
SELECT and JOIN identify relatives and connect records, while GROUP BY, COUNT(), and AVG() construct multi-year earnings measures.
Using PSID data, the IGE increases from 0.0322 to 0.0641 when moving from single-year to multi-year earnings within the same 1,027 mother–child pairs.
However, the paired-bootstrap difference is not statistically significant.
A stricter balanced sample of 489 pairs shows that single-year IGE estimates vary between 0.0051 and 0.0558 across four income years.
Age-group comparisons further suggest that the timing of income measurement may be particularly important when parental earnings are observed near retirement.
The broader lesson is that intergenerational mobility estimates depend not only on the regression model but also on how individuals are matched and how economic status is measured.
Careful SQL matching, transparent aggregation, consistent samples, and explicit treatment of measurement uncertainty are essential for credible longitudinal analysis.

text:
Do children from higher-earning families tend to earn more as adults? Answering this question requires two tasks: identifying parents and children in longitudinal records, and measuring earnings in a way that reflects long-run economic status. A single year can be unusually good or bad, and earnings change as people enter the labor market or retire.
Research question: How can SQL inside Python match mothers and adult children in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), and how sensitive is the estimated intergenerational earnings elasticity (IGE) to using one year versus several years of earnings?
This tutorial moves from identifiers to SQL joins, constructs individual earnings, uses SQL aggregation to average earnings, estimates the IGE, and examines measurement-year and maternal-age sensitivity.
The analysis concerns birth mothers’ and adult children’s individual labor earnings, not total parental household income or causal effects.

section: 2. SQL Inside Python: Match Birth Mothers and Children
text:
2. SQL Inside Python: Match Birth Mothers and Children
Python’s built-in sqlite3 package runs SQL without requiring a separate database server.
The following teaching example illustrates the key operations. It assumes that the earlier cleaning steps produced DataFrames pid_df and individual_df with the original PSID identifier columns.
The complete executable pipeline is in code/03_sql_matching.py.

import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as conn:

    pid_df.to_sql(
        "pid",
        conn,
        index=False,
        if_exists="replace"
    )

    individual_df.to_sql(
        "individuals",
        conn,
        index=False,
        if_exists="replace"
    )

    pairs = pd.read_sql_query(
        """
        SELECT DISTINCT
            p.PID2 AS child_interview_id,
            p.PID3 AS child_person_number,
            p.PID4 AS mother_interview_id,
            p.PID5 AS mother_person_number

        FROM pid AS p

        INNER JOIN individuals AS c
            ON p.PID2 = c.ER30001
           AND p.PID3 = c.ER30002

        INNER JOIN individuals AS m
            ON p.PID4 = m.ER30001
           AND p.PID5 = m.ER30002

        WHERE p.PID4 IS NOT NULL
          AND p.PID5 IS NOT NULL
        """,
        conn
    )


Understanding SELECT and JOIN
SELECT chooses the variables needed for the analysis, while AS assigns readable names.
The first INNER JOIN checks whether the child appears in the individual records.
The second INNER JOIN checks whether the birth mother also appears.
Each join uses both components of the individual identifier. Matching on only one component could incorrectly link unrelated individuals.
WHERE excludes records without usable maternal identifiers, and DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows.
An INNER JOIN retains only successful matches.
A LEFT JOIN, in contrast, preserves unmatched rows from the left-hand table.


Why not match on family ID alone?
A child and mother may live in different households as the child grows up.
Their current family IDs therefore need not match, and family IDs are not stable individual identifiers.
The matching pipeline identifies 41,839 unique mother–child identifier pairs.
After restricting to adult children aged 25 or older and pairs with age information for both generations in 2023, the working sample contains 4,242 pairs.
These are candidate relationships, not yet the regression sample. Earnings requirements further reduce the number of observations.

3. Link Person-Years to Earnings
After identifying relatives, we connect each individual-year observation to the correct family interview record.
The join requires both the family ID and the interview year because a family interview identifier is not a permanent person identifier.

LEFT JOIN retains person-year observations even when the family earnings record is unavailable, making missingness visible rather than silently discarding observations.

section: 4. GROUP BY and Aggregation: Construct Multi-Year Earnings
text:
4. GROUP BY and Aggregation: Construct Multi-Year Earnings
A single observed earnings year may reflect a temporary shock.
We therefore construct a second earnings measure: each person’s average observed positive labor earnings across the four income reference years.

# income_panel is the cleaned person-year earnings DataFrame.

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as conn:

    income_panel.to_sql(
        "income_panel",
        conn,
        index=False,
        if_exists="replace"
    )

    average_earnings = pd.read_sql_query(
        """
        SELECT
            interview_id,
            person_number,
            COUNT(*) AS n_positive_years,
            AVG(individual_income) AS avg_income,
            MIN(income_year) AS first_income_year,
            MAX(income_year) AS last_income_year

        FROM income_panel

        WHERE individual_income > 0

        GROUP BY
            interview_id,
            person_number
        """,
        conn
    )


Understanding GROUP BY and Aggregation
WHERE individual_income > 0 selects positive earnings observations before aggregation.
GROUP BY collects multiple year records belonging to the same individual.
COUNT(*) counts qualifying earnings observations, while AVG() calculates their arithmetic mean.
MIN() and MAX() identify the earliest and latest earnings years observed.
We require at least two positive-income observations for both the mother and child in the primary multi-year specification.


Why Average Earnings?
Suppose an individual’s observed earnings can be written as:
\[
Y_{it} = Y_i^{long-run} + u_{it}
\]
where \(Y_i^{long-run}\) represents long-run earnings and \(u_{it}\) represents a temporary income fluctuation.
Averaging over several years gives:
\[
\bar{Y}_i =
Y_i^{long-run}
+
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}u_{it}
\]
If temporary fluctuations partly offset one another, averaging can reduce their influence.
However, this study averages positive observed nominal labor earnings, not lifetime income.
Excluding zero-income years creates selection concerns, and the averages are not adjusted for inflation.
These limitations matter when interpreting the IGE.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
5. Estimate the Intergenerational Earnings Elasticity
We estimate the following log–log OLS regression:
\[
\ln(Y_i^{child})
=
\alpha
+
\beta\ln(Y_i^{mother})
+
\varepsilon_i
\]
where:

\(Y_i^{child}\) is the adult child’s labor earnings.
\(Y_i^{mother}\) is the birth mother’s labor earnings.
\(\alpha\) is the intercept.
\(\beta\) is the intergenerational earnings elasticity.
\(\varepsilon_i\) represents other factors associated with child earnings.

The coefficient \(\beta\) measures the percentage association between maternal and adult-child earnings.
For example, if \(\beta = 0.10\), a 1% increase in maternal earnings is associated with approximately 0.10% higher child earnings.
A larger positive IGE indicates stronger measured earnings persistence across generations.
Importantly, this coefficient is descriptive rather than causal.
We report HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and approximate 95% confidence intervals.

6. Life-Cycle Bias: Why Age at Measurement Matters
Labor earnings vary over the life cycle.
They may be relatively low early in a career, rise with experience, and decline when working hours decrease or retirement begins.
As a result, income observed at a particular age may not accurately represent an individual’s long-run earning capacity.
This creates the possibility of life-cycle bias in estimated intergenerational earnings persistence.
For example, a mother who earned relatively high income during her working years may report low labor earnings after retirement.
If researchers observe only her retirement-year earnings, they may underestimate her earlier economic status.

What Does Figure 5 Show?
The single-year IGE varies from 0.0051 in 2018 to 0.0558 in 2022, even though the mother–child pairs remain exactly the same.
This demonstrates that the estimated relationship between maternal and child earnings is sensitive to the income measurement year.
A researcher observing only 2018 earnings would obtain a much smaller IGE point estimate than a researcher observing only 2022 earnings.
The multi-year IGE is 0.0432, which lies within the range of the single-year estimates.
Importantly, multi-year averaging does not necessarily produce a larger IGE.
Its purpose is to reduce the influence of temporary earnings fluctuations, not to mechanically increase the estimated coefficient.
The confidence intervals indicate considerable statistical uncertainty.
The multi-year estimate’s 95% confidence interval includes zero, and we have not conducted a formal paired test of all four yearly coefficients.
Therefore, the observed differences should not be interpreted as statistically significant without additional testing.
Furthermore, year-specific economic shocks may affect earnings alongside changes in age.
Figure 5 demonstrates measurement-year sensitivity, while Figure 4 provides complementary evidence about maternal age.
Together, they illustrate why single-point income measurement can create problems for studying intergenerational mobility, although they do not isolate a causal life-cycle effect.
